lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
List two respectful learning actions and one action to avoid when studying First Nations music.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Use approved sources; credit community/source. Avoid: inventing sacred songs or copying restricted practices.'

WATCH FOR
Treating First Nations music as one single style or as free costume play. Diversity and protocols matter.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Using only teacher-approved sources, write five verified facts about First Nations music or instruments and two questions for Community educators. No performance of restricted material.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teach_steps.explain:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have diverse music traditions, instruments and song knowledge across many Countries. Some songs, ceremonies and instrument practices are restricted. This lesson focuses on respectful awareness using only published, classroom-approved materials chosen with guidance from Aboriginal educators where possible. Name Country or community only when the source does. Do not invent Dreaming stories, imitate sacred song or build pretend ceremonial instruments.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the elements, techniques or performance choices that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. For movement or instruments, use a clear space, ask an adult to be nearby and stop if anything feels unsafe. You may always describe a choice instead of performing it. One deliberate artistic choice with a named effect is more useful than a longer praise sentence.
